title: Spectral Perturbation Bounds for Low-Rank Approximation with Applications

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3, Lemma 3.1 and derivation of Theorem 2.1
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Lemma 3.1 is stated under the stronger condition "δ_p > 5||E||", but Theorem 2.1 assumes only "4||E|| < δ_p" and is claimed to follow from the lemma. Thus the stated lemma cannot establish the theorem over the interval 4||E|| < δ_p <= 5||E||. The proof of the lemma itself instead uses only 4||E|| < δ_p, contradicting its own statement. The assumptions and theorem derivation must be made consistent.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3, estimation of M_1 in the proof outline of Theorem 2.1
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper claims directly that ∫_{-T}^T sqrt(x_0^2+t^2)/((δ_p/2)^2+t^2) dt = O(x_0/δ_p). This omits an unavoidable logarithmic contribution. For |t| substantially larger than δ_p and up to T, the integrand is asymptotically 1/|t|, producing a term of order log(T/δ_p). With T=2λ_1, this logarithm can be arbitrarily large relative to λ_p/δ_p. The asserted O(||E|| λ_p/δ_p) bound therefore does not follow from the displayed contour estimate.

The displayed resolvent identity has the wrong sign: for R_A=(zI-A)^{-1} and R_tilde=(zI-A-E)^{-1}, the correct identity is R_tilde-R_A=R_A E R_tilde (equivalently R_A-R_tilde=-R_A E R_tilde). The paper writes R_A-R_tilde=R_A E R_tilde. Norms can hide the sign in later inequalities, but the claimed matrix identity and the subsequent algebra are incorrect as written.

predicted_errors.error_location: Theorem 2.3 and its description in Section 2
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper calls f_p(A)=Σ_{i<=p}f(λ_i)u_i u_i^T "the best rank-p approximation of f(A)" for general analytic functions, including trigonometric functions. This is false in general: the best rank-p approximation in spectral/Frobenius norm retains the p largest singular values |f(λ_i)|, not necessarily f evaluated on the p largest eigenvalues of A. For example, f(z)=cos z is nonmonotone and can make a lower eigenvalue have larger |f(λ)| than a leading eigenvalue. The contour identity may concern the selected leading-eigenvalue functional, but it does not establish the claimed best-rank-p result.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix F, proof of Theorem 2.3, bounds on M_2 and M_4
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The proof states |x_1-x_0|/T^2 <= λ_1/(4λ_1^2). But x_1=2λ_1 and x_0=λ_p-δ_p/2, so x_1-x_0 can be close to 2λ_1, not at most λ_1/4. Consequently the stated M_2,M_4 bounds are false. Although a weaker constant may still suffice for a repaired final estimate, the supplied proof is invalid.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix D, Theorems D.1 and D.5
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The symmetric extensions are stated for arbitrary k with 1<=k<=p, but use δ_{n-(p-k)}. When p-k=0 (in particular, when all selected singular directions are positive, the ordinary PSD case), this becomes δ_n, which was defined only for indices 1,...,n-1 and is undefined. The claimed general theorem therefore is not well-defined in an included, common case.

The introduction defines for a general real symmetric matrix A the top-eigenvalue truncation A_p=Σ_{i=1}^p λ_i u_i u_i^T and claims it solves the best rank-p approximation problem. This is false for indefinite matrices: best rank-p approximation retains eigencomponents with largest absolute eigenvalues/singular values. Appendix D correctly recognizes this issue and defines the selected components using the top singular values, contradicting the introduction's general symmetric-matrix claim.

predicted_errors.error_location: Theorem 2.2 versus Appendix H notation table
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Theorem 2.2 defines r as the smallest integer with λ_{r+1} <= λ_p/2. Appendix H instead defines the halving distance as the smallest integer satisfying "λ_{p/2} >= λ_{r+1}". These are different conditions and the latter is not even coherent for arbitrary integer p. Since r is central to Theorem 2.2, the paper gives incompatible definitions.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4, experimental setting and result paragraph
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Adult covariance matrix is first reported as having n=14 (and p=4), but later the same experiment is described as a "6 × 6 Adult matrix" and uses n=6 in the gap calculation. No explicit dimensional reduction reconcilles these statements is reported in the setting. The reported dataset/matrix dimension is internally inconsistent.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4, paragraph asserting spectral regularization establishes the gap condition
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper says that adding "0.1·λ_1·I" to the covariance matrix makes the eigengap condition 4||E||<δ_p hold. Adding a scalar multiple of the identity shifts every eigenvalue by the same amount and leaves every eigengap δ_p=λ_p-λ_{p+1} exactly unchanged. This preprocessing cannot improve the stated gap condition.

The protocol specifies 3 datasets × 2 noise models × 20 levels × 100 trials = 12,000 trials. It then says that 12 outlier trials constitute "1.3%". Twelve out of 12,000 is 0.1%, not 1.3%. Even if the synthetic dataset were excluded from the stated result, 12 out of 12,000 remains the relevant count for the explicitly described benchmark protocol.

The paper says it excluded 12 trials where the bound exceeded the error by "more than 10×," but immediately claims that over all benchmark experiments its estimate "never deviates from the observed error by more than a single order of magnitude." An error ratio greater than 10 is, by definition, greater than one order of magnitude. Excluding observations cannot support an unqualified claim over all experiments.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4, treatment of excluded outliers and final empirical conclusion
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper removes trials precisely because the theoretical upper bound was more than 10 times the actual error, then uses the filtered results to assert "uniform tightness," "practically sharp" behavior, and an application-agnostic certificate. Excluding unfavorable trials without a pre-specified exclusion rule or reporting the full distribution makes the tightness conclusion unsupported; numerical instability of a bound evaluated from finite matrices is not a valid justification for deleting valid trials.

The appendix writes E=α·N(0,I_n) for a covariance-matrix perturbation while applying eigenvalue/eigengap theory that requires E to be symmetric. N(0,I_n) conventionally denotes an n-dimensional Gaussian vector, and if interpreted as an iid Gaussian matrix it is not symmetric. Unlike the main experiments, this setup never specifies GOE symmetrization, so the stated perturbation model is not sufficiently defined to support the spectral analysis.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2 and Section 4 citations [41,43] for Wigner spectral-norm asymptotics
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Reference [41] is Van Huffel and Vandewalle, "On the accuracy of total least squares and least squares techniques in the presence of errors on all data" (Automatica, 1989). It is not a result on spectral norms of Wigner/sub-Gaussian random matrices and cannot support the repeated claim that ||E||=(2+o(1))sqrt(n) for Wigner noise. The relevant cited source may be [43], but [41] is misattributed.

The introduction says the question was raised in "[29, Remark 5.3] and [30, Section 6.2]," but later claims to resolve the question posed in "[30, Remark 5.3]." These are incompatible specific attributions. At least one citation location is wrong and must be checked.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix D.1, Lemma D.4 and Appendix E.2
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Lemma D.4 states N_2,N_4 <= sqrt(2(a_1-a_0))/T, whereas Appendix E.2 derives N_2,N_4 <= sqrt(2)|a_1-a_0|/T. These expressions are materially different (and the Lemma D.4 expression has inconsistent scaling). The subsequent proof uses a constant consistent with the Appendix E.2 form, not with the lemma as stated.
